questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches over the trunk and upper limbs. Slit skin smear shows numerous acid-fast bacilli. Histopathology reveals a continuous granulomatous band along the dermo-epidermal junction with no Grenz zone. Which type of leprosy does this represent?
questions.exp: Lepromatous leprosy (LL) shows heavily bacilli-laden macrophages (Virchow cells), a continuous granulomatous band in the dermis with a clear Grenz zone (subepidermal clear zone). The absence of a Grenz zone described here would actually be TT/BT, but the numerous AFBs and continuous granuloma pattern fits LL. LL has high bacterial load, symmetrical lesions, and a clear Grenz zone separating infiltrate from epidermis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent painful oral ulcers and genital ulcers for 6 months, along with bilateral anterior uveitis. She also has tender nodules on her shins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Behçet's disease is characterised by the triad of recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. Additional features include skin manifestations like erythema nodosum and pseudofolliculitis. It is associated with HLA-B51 and is more prevalent in Turkey, Middle East, and East Asia (Silk Road disease).

questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with a painless papule on the right forearm that developed after a thorn prick 3 weeks ago. It has evolved into an ulcer with a black eschar surrounded by non-pitting oedema. Gram stain of the eschar shows large Gram-positive rods in chains. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: This is cutaneous anthrax caused by Bacillus anthracis (large Gram-positive rods in chains). The classic presentation is a painless ulcer with black eschar ('malignant pustule') and surrounding non-pitting oedema. Penicillin G is the drug of choice for cutaneous anthrax. Ciprofloxacin and doxycycline are alternatives for bioterrorism-related anthrax.

questions.q: A 22-year-old sexually active male presents with painless inguinal lymphadenopathy. On examination, the nodes are hard, rubbery, and non-tender, arranged in a 'chain of beads' pattern. There is no primary genital ulcer. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3 presents with painless inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes) arranged in a 'groove sign' (nodes above and below the inguinal ligament) or chain-like pattern. The primary papule/ulcer is transient and often missed. Treatment is doxycycline for 21 days.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man on long-term corticosteroids for pemphigus vulgaris develops sudden-onset haemoptysis and cavitating lung lesions. Skin examination reveals multiple painless nodules and verrucous plaques on the face. KOH mount from skin scraping shows broad-based budding yeast with thick capsule. What is the organism?
questions.exp: Blastomycosis (Blastomyces dermatitidis) presents with pulmonary involvement and characteristic verrucous skin lesions on the face. The yeast shows broad-based budding (single bud) on KOH mount, distinguishing it from Cryptococcus (narrow-based, capsulated) and Candida (pseudohyphae). It is a dimorphic fungus endemic to North America.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on erythematous skin of the trunk and extremities. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposits along the basement membrane zone. The N-terminal domain of BP180 (NC16A) is the target antigen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common autoimmune bullous disorder in adults. It presents with tense bullae on erythematous or urticarial base. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ. Target antigens are BP180 (type XVII collagen, NC16A domain) and BP230. It is subepidermal on histology, unlike pemphigus (intraepidermal).

questions.q: A 40-year-old man presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales on the elbows, knees, and scalp. He has pitting of nails and is HLA-Cw6 positive. Joint X-ray shows 'pencil-in-cup' deformity. Which joints are most commonly affected?
questions.exp: Psoriatic arthritis most commonly affects the DIP (distal interphalangeal) joints, which is a distinguishing feature from rheumatoid arthritis (affects MCPs and PIPs). The 'pencil-in-cup' deformity on X-ray is pathognomonic of psoriatic arthritis. HLA-Cw6 is associated with plaque psoriasis.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along a dermatomal distribution over the left thorax, associated with severe burning pain. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. After resolution of the rash, the patient continues to have severe pain for more than 3 months. What is this complication called?
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is defined as pain persisting for >3 months after resolution of herpes zoster rash. It is the most common complication of herpes zoster, particularly in elderly patients. Ramsay Hunt syndrome involves the geniculate ganglion (CN VII) with ear vesicles and facial palsy. Treatment of PHN includes gabapentin, pregabalin, tricyclic antidepressants, and topical lidocaine.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and polyarthritis. ANA is positive (1:640, homogeneous pattern). Anti-dsDNA antibodies are strongly positive. Skin biopsy from normal sun-protected skin shows immunoglobulin deposits at the DEJ. This finding is called:
questions.exp: The lupus band test (LBT) refers to the deposition of immunoglobulins (IgG, IgM, IgA) and complement at the dermal-epidermal junction on direct immunofluorescence. A positive LBT from non-sun-exposed, non-lesional skin is highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Anti-dsDNA antibodies are specific for SLE and correlate with disease activity.

questions.q: A 20-year-old male presents with a 2 cm indurated, painless ulcer on the shaft of penis for 3 weeks with associated non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy of exudate shows motile spirochaetes. RPR titre is 1:64. What is the treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: This is primary syphilis (painless chancre + non-tender lymphadenopathy) caused by Treponema pallidum. Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose is the treatment of choice for primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis. Doxycycline 100mg BD for 14 days is used for penicillin-allergic patients. RPR is a non-treponemal test useful for treatment monitoring.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with large, fleshy, painless nodules on the genitalia and perineum that bleed on contact. Histopathology shows Donovan bodies (intracytoplasmic inclusions in mononuclear cells). What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis). It presents with painless, beefy-red, friable vegetating ulcers that bleed easily on contact. Donovan bodies are bipolar staining intracytoplasmic inclusions in mononuclear cells seen on Giemsa or Wright stain. Treatment: azithromycin or doxycycline for minimum 3 weeks.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with recurrent blistering of sun-exposed skin. He is a known case of hepatitis C. On examination, there is skin fragility, milia formation, hyperpigmentation, and hypertrichosis on the face. Urine shows pink-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) is the most common porphyria. It is caused by reduced uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity. Features include skin fragility, bullae on sun-exposed areas, milia, hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis on face. Associated with hepatitis C, alcohol, iron overload, and oestrogens. Urine shows pink-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp due to uroporphyrin. Treatment: phlebotomy and low-dose hydroxychloroquine.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. The lesions began as vesicles that ruptured to form golden crusts. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. What is the first-line topical treatment?
questions.exp: This is impetigo, most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (Gram-positive cocci in clusters). The classic presentation is honey-coloured crusted lesions. Topical mupirocin 2% is the first-line treatment for localised impetigo. Fusidic acid is an alternative. Systemic antibiotics (flucloxacillin, cephalexin) are used for extensive disease. Mupirocin works by inhibiting isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase.

questions.q: A 25-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 50/μL) presents with multiple, painless, skin-coloured to pink umbilicated papules all over the face, trunk, and extremities, measuring 2-6mm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum (MC) caused by a poxvirus presents with umbilicated pearly papules. In immunocompetent individuals it is self-limiting, but in HIV patients with low CD4 counts, MC can be extensive, giant-sized, and disfiguring, particularly on the face. The molluscum body (Henderson-Paterson body) is seen on histopathology. Treatment in HIV: HAART leads to resolution; local destructive therapies can be used.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with violaceous flat-topped polygonal papules over the flexor aspects of wrists and ankles, associated with intense pruritus. White lacy patterns are seen on the buccal mucosa. Histopathology shows 'saw-tooth' acanthosis, hypergranulosis, and band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the DEJ. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lichen planus presents with the 5 P's: Pruritic, Purple, Polygonal, Planar (flat-topped) Papules. Wickham's striae are white lacy patterns on mucosa. Histopathology shows: hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, irregular 'saw-tooth' acanthosis, vacuolar degeneration of basal cells, and band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at DEJ with Civatte (colloid) bodies. Koebner phenomenon is positive.

questions.q: A 30-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques that started on the abdomen (sparing the umbilicus) and spread to the thighs. She has no fever or systemic symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy (PUPPP)
questions.exp: PUPPP (polymorphic eruption of pregnancy) is the most common specific dermatosis of pregnancy. It typically occurs in the third trimester, starts within abdominal striae (striae gravidarum) and characteristically SPARES the umbilicus. It is benign and self-limiting. Pemphigoid gestationis starts periumbilically, has tense bullae, and shows linear C3 on DIF.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectatic vessels on the nose. The nodule has a rolled border and central ulceration. Sun exposure history is significant. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment of choice?
opts: Squamous cell carcinoma; wide local excision
Basal cell carcinoma; Mohs micrographic surgery
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin cancer. Nodular BCC presents as a pearly translucent nodule with telangiectasia and rolled borders on sun-exposed areas, particularly the nose (H-zone). Mohs micrographic surgery offers the highest cure rate (99%) with maximal tissue conservation and is preferred for high-risk locations (face, H-zone) and recurrent BCCs. BCC rarely metastasizes.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with scaling erythematous patches in the sebaceous gland-rich areas: scalp, nasolabial folds, chest, and back. KOH examination of scale shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: This is seborrhoeic dermatitis, associated with Malassezia furfur (formerly Pityrosporum ovale). KOH mount showing 'spaghetti and meatballs' is classic for pityriasis versicolor (also caused by Malassezia), and seborrhoeic dermatitis has a similar pathogen. Topical antifungals (ketoconazole 2% shampoo, selenium sulfide) are first-line. Griseofulvin is for dermatophytoses, not Malassezia.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man presents with hypopigmented macules on the chest and upper back. Wood's lamp examination shows apple-green fluorescence. KOH mount reveals short, curved hyphae and round spores. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia species (dimorphic lipophilic yeast). It presents with hypopigmented or hyperpigmented scaly macules on trunk. KOH mount shows the pathognomonic 'spaghetti and meatballs' (short curved hyphae + round spores). Wood's lamp shows golden-yellow fluorescence (not apple-green, which is for Microsporum). Treatment: topical selenium sulphide, ketoconazole; oral fluconazole/itraconazole for extensive disease.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents with an erythematous scaly plaque with irregular borders on the forearm that has been slowly enlarging over 2 years. Dermoscopy shows dotted vessels and white structureless areas. Biopsy shows full-thickness dysplasia of the epidermis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bowen's disease is squamous cell carcinoma in situ. Histopathology shows full-thickness dysplasia (atypical keratinocytes throughout the entire epidermis) with an intact basement membrane. It presents as a slowly enlarging erythematous scaly plaque. Actinic keratosis shows partial thickness dysplasia. Treatment: topical 5-FU, imiquimod, cryotherapy, PDT, or surgical excision.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman develops severe mucocutaneous blistering 3 weeks after starting a new medication for seizures. She has involvement of >30% BSA with epidermal detachment, and the Nikolsky sign is positive. What is the most likely drug implicated?
questions.exp: Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) with >30% BSA involvement is most commonly caused by aromatic anticonvulsants, particularly carbamazepine. Other common culprits include allopurinol, sulphonamides, NSAIDs, and lamotrigine. Carbamazepine-induced TEN is associated with HLA-B*15:02 in Asian patients. SCORTEN is used to predict mortality. Withdraw offending drug; manage in a burns unit.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, skin tightening of the fingers extending to the elbows, and telangiectasias. She has anti-centromere antibodies. Which organ involvement determines prognosis?
questions.exp: This describes limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc, formerly CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Oesophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia). Anti-centromere antibodies are characteristic. Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is the leading cause of death in lcSSc. In diffuse SSc, scleroderma renal crisis (with anti-Scl-70/anti-topoisomerase I antibodies) is the main concern.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of wheals and angioedema since childhood. Episodes are precipitated by minor trauma and do not respond to antihistamines. C4 levels are persistently low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) is an autosomal dominant condition due to C1 inhibitor deficiency (Type I) or dysfunction (Type II). It presents with recurrent non-pitting, non-pruritic angioedema without wheals, often precipitated by trauma or stress. C4 is persistently low (screening test). Antihistamines are ineffective. Acute treatment: C1-INH concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), or fresh frozen plasma.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with diffuse hair loss following childbirth 3 months ago. She notices excessive shedding while combing. Examination shows no scarring or inflammation. Hair pull test yields >6 hairs easily. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Telogen effluvium (TE) is diffuse non-scarring hair loss that occurs 2-4 months after a triggering event (childbirth, surgery, severe illness, rapid weight loss, thyroid disease). Post-partum TE is very common. It is due to a synchronised shift of hair follicles from anagen to telogen. The hair pull test is positive (>6 hairs). It is usually self-limiting and resolves within 6-9 months.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man undergoing treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis develops a maculo-papular rash 6 weeks after starting 4-drug ATT. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Rifampicin is the most common cause of cutaneous reactions among ATT drugs, including maculopapular rash, urticaria, and pruritus. It also causes drug hypersensitivity reactions and flu-like syndrome with intermittent therapy. Isoniazid causes pellagra-like dermatitis (pyridoxine deficiency). Pyrazinamide causes photosensitivity and rash. Proper identification is important for drug de-challenge and rechallenge.

questions.q: A biopsy from a skin lesion is subjected to direct immunofluorescence. It shows granular IgA deposits at the tips of dermal papillae. What is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is characterised by granular IgA deposits at the tips of dermal papillae on DIF. It presents with intensely pruritic grouped vesicles over extensor surfaces (elbows, knees, buttocks). It is associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy (coeliac disease) and HLA-DQ2/DQ8. Treatment: gluten-free diet (definitive) and dapsone (symptomatic). Linear IgA shows linear IgA along BMZ.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with an erythematous annular plaque with central clearing and an active, scaly, vesicular border on the forearm. KOH mount shows septate hyphae. What is the investigation of choice to confirm dermatophyte infection?
questions.exp: Culture on Sabouraud's dextrose agar (SDA) with cycloheximide and chloramphenicol is the gold standard for confirming dermatophyte species. KOH mount demonstrates hyphae and confirms the diagnosis clinically, but culture identifies the species. Wood's lamp shows blue-green fluorescence for Microsporum species (not Trichophyton, the most common cause of tinea corporis). PAS stain is used on histopathology.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with a painless 2 cm skin-coloured to brownish soft subcutaneous nodule on the forearm. He recalls it appeared after a minor cut while working in a garden. FNAC reveals thick-walled, brown, 'copper penny' (muriform) cells dividing by cross-wall formation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis presents with verrucous, cauliflower-like nodules and plaques typically on lower limbs following inoculation trauma. The pathognomonic finding is 'sclerotic bodies' (Medlar bodies/muriform cells/copper penny cells) – thick-walled, dark brown, dividing by septation in multiple planes – in histopathology or FNAC. Caused by dematiaceous fungi (Fonsecaea pedrosoi). Treatment: itraconazole ± terbinafine.

questions.q: During a leprosy examination, you notice that a patient's auricular nerve is visibly thickened and palpable. The patient has a single hypopigmented anaesthetic patch. What type of leprosy does this represent?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) presents with one or a few well-defined, hypopigmented, anaesthetic macules or plaques with raised edges. The nearest cutaneous nerve is thickened, and common nerves like the great auricular, ulnar, and common peroneal nerves may be prominently thickened. AFB are absent or very few. The immune response is strong (Th1-mediated). The great auricular nerve is the most visible and easily palpable peripheral nerve.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman on hydroxychloroquine for SLE presents with a characteristic 'bull's eye' or 'target' lesion pattern on fundoscopy. What is this side effect?
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) can cause retinal toxicity characterised by a 'bull's eye' maculopathy on fundoscopy and visual field defects. This is dose and duration dependent (risk increases with >5mg/kg/day and >5 years of use). Annual ophthalmological screening (preferably with OCT and 10-2 visual field testing) is recommended. Corneal microdeposits (vortex keratopathy) also occur but are benign and reversible.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a 2×3 cm verrucous plaque on the dorsum of the foot. Biopsy shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with intraepidermal abscesses containing neutrophils and eosinophils (Pautrier-like abscesses with polymorphs). Grains are found in the dermis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Mycetoma (Madura foot) presents as a tumour-like swelling with sinuses discharging grains. Eumycetoma (fungal) shows grains on histopathology. Pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia is seen. White/yellow grains: Madurella grisea, Aspergillus; black grains: Madurella mycetomatis; red grains: actinomycetes. Distinguished from chromoblastomycosis which shows muriform cells. Treatment of eumycetoma: itraconazole ± surgical debulking.
